posts.title: Cooking the syrups at seven
posts.excerpt: Four small pans, one wooden spoon each, and the windows open to the garden.
posts.content:
The fruit arrives at half past six. By seven the strawberries are in the copper pan with a handful of sugar and nothing else, and the kitchen smells like June.

We stop the heat while the colour is still bright. A syrup cooked too long tastes of jam, and jam is too heavy for snow.

posts.title: Why the matcha is whisked last
posts.excerpt: Matcha loses its green in an hour, so we whisk it for each bowl.
posts.content:
Most parlours keep a jug of matcha syrup in the fridge. It is easier, but by the afternoon it has turned the colour of moss and tastes flat.

We whisk a spoon of powder with warm syrup in a small bowl while the ice is shaved. It takes thirty seconds and you can see the difference from the door.

posts.title: Tea flowers, bees and next year’s honey
posts.excerpt: The tea hedge flowers in late autumn, and the hives work right up to the frost.
posts.content:
We planted tea bushes along the back fence the year we opened. Now they make a dark green hedge, and when the small white flowers open in October the bees from our two hives hardly leave it.

In January, when the pond ice is cut in the mountains, we wrap the hives in straw. The honey from those flowers is what softens the yuzu bowl the next summer.
